title: Birha: longing
hook: the ache of separation is honored in the Granth as part of love

segments.voice: Yesterday, suhagan, the bride united with her beloved. Your line was the soul is a bride. Did you read your line of longing again last night? Today, the longing itself, and the end of a week. Day two hundred forty-five.

Think of an airport arrivals hall. People holding signs, holding flowers, craning their necks at the sliding doors. Some have waited months. Nobody would say those people love less because they're waiting. If anything, the waiting is the love, made visible. Most of us treat missing someone, or missing God, as a problem to fix fast. The Guru Granth Sahib does something unexpected with that ache. It doesn't hide it. It honors it, and gives it a name. Today's word: birha.

Birha is the pain of separation: the bride from the beloved, the soul from God. Yesterday's bride was united. Today's bride is at the window, still waiting. And the Granth gives her a lot of room. Guru Arjan's Barah Maha walks through the twelve months of the year, and in month after month the bride aches for her beloved, in the heat, in the rains, in the cold. Guru Nanak has his own Barah Maha too. The longing isn't treated as failure. It's treated as a sign that love is alive. The boldest line comes from Sheikh Farid, a Sufi poet of the Punjab whose couplets the Gurus kept in the Granth; we'll meet him properly in two weeks. He says, in the original: birhaa birhaa aakheeai birhaa too sultaan. People keep saying separation, separation; separation, you are the king. And then: the body in which this longing never rises, know it as a cremation ground. Strong words. The ache, Farid says, is proof of life. A heart that never misses anything isn't peaceful. It's asleep. Why would a tradition honor pain? Because longing points. You can only miss what you love. So in the Granth, birha is not the opposite of love. It's love, facing the door. That's the week's thread, too. This week: the five thieves and the five virtues, maya's passing pull, facing the Guru, the ease of sahaj, the soul as a bride, and now birha. Every one of them is about where the heart is facing.
screen: `BIRHA — THE ACHE OF SEPARATION.` · `TWELVE MONTHS OF WAITING.` · `FARID: SEPARATION, YOU ARE KING.` · `YOU ONLY MISS WHAT YOU LOVE.` · then, large: `LONGING IS LOVE TOO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one longing you carry: a person far away, someone who has died, a hope that hasn't come, or, if you pray, a longing for God. Don't try to fix it or push it away. Sit beside it, kindly, the way you'd sit beside a friend in an arrivals hall. Let it be what it is: a sign of love. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Birha. The ache of separation, honored in the Granth as part of love. This week's words: the five thieves, the five virtues, maya, gurmukh, sahaj, suhagan, birha.
Your line: longing is love too. Today, when you miss someone or something, don't rush past it; let it remind you what you love. Day two hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Hymns of longing, including the Barah Maha of the twelve months, are sung in Sikh kirtan; many gurdwaras recite the Barah Maha in Majh on sangrand, the first day of each month in the Punjabi calendar.

fork.setup: you're aching for someone you can't reach. what does the Granth's picture of birha suggest?
options: treat the ache as a sign of love, and sit with it kindly.
fork.reveal: Farid calls separation the king: a heart that never longs is asleep. you only miss what you love.

original.note: Gurmukhi: birha, the pain of separation; Farid's salok calls it sultaan, the king.

trapdoor: what you thought: longing means something is wrong.
what it means: in the Granth, the ache of separation is part of love, and a heart that never longs is asleep.
what a scholar hears: birha is a central mood of Punjabi and Sufi poetry; Farid's salok (Ang 1379) crowns it sultaan, and the Barah Maha genre maps it onto the twelve months.
